deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate research notes. Each is a problem or programme with at most a proof sketch; none contains a worked calculation.

(1) DIOPHANTINE PROGRAMME FOR 2^{sqrt2}.
The task: approximate (1-z)^a and (1-z)^{-a} simultaneously by rational functions with one common denominator.
- Modern form (type-II Hermite-Pade problem): find polynomials P_n, Q_n, R_n of degree <= n, with P_n not 0, such that
  P_n(z)(1-z)^a - Q_n(z) = O(z^{m}) and P_n(z)(1-z)^{-a} - R_n(z) = O(z^{m}), with m about 3n/2.
- The coefficients of P, Q, R are polynomials in a with rational coefficients, because binomial(a,k) is a polynomial in a.
- Specialise to z = -1 and a = sqrt2. Then (1-z)^a = 2^{sqrt2} and (1-z)^{-a} = 2^{-sqrt2}.
- Since 1-z has its branch point at z = 1, both binomial series and their Pade-type approximants make sense at z = -1. (I take the specialisation z = -1 as intended; the text says only 'z. B.'.)
- Implicit idea (my reading): the coefficients lie in Q(sqrt2). The Galois conjugation sqrt2 -> -sqrt2 swaps the two functions. A common denominator therefore lets one form linear forms L_n = P_n(-1)*2^{sqrt2} - Q_n(-1) whose conjugates are the companion forms.
- If 2^{sqrt2} = p/q were rational, then 2^{-sqrt2} = q/p as well. Then N(L_n) (or q*L_n) would be a nonzero element of bounded denominator that tends to 0, a contradiction.
- This is exactly the Thue-Siegel scheme: Thue (1909) used Pade approximants of (1-z)^{1/n}.
- Smallest case, worked by me: the [1/1] Pade approximant of (1-z)^a is (1-(a+1)z/2)/(1-(1-a)z/2). That of (1-z)^{-a} is its reciprocal (1-(1-a)z/2)/(1-(1+a)z/2). So the two diagonal problems are 'conjugate' under a -> -a, which is presumably what Hilbert noticed.

(2) CLASS FIELD THEORY FOR FUNCTION FIELDS.
Claim: every extension that is relatively abelian over an algebraic function field K (of one variable, over C) is obtained by division of the abelian functions belonging to K.
- Modern reading: the abelian functions are functions on the Jacobian J of the curve X.
- Division means adjoining the pullbacks under the Abel-Jacobi map X -> J of the coordinates of [n]^{-1}, i.e. of the n-division points.
- This yields the maximal abelian unramified extension of exponent n.
- This is the function-field analogue of the Kronecker Jugendtraum and of the 12th Paris problem: division values of elliptic/abelian functions generate abelian extensions.
- No proof is given.

(3) DIVISOR CLASSES SUPPORTED IN AN ARBITRARY OPEN SET.
Claim: in every arbitrarily small region U of a Riemann surface X there are points P_1, ..., P_r whose product (as prime ideals) lies in a prescribed ideal class.
Proof sketch:
- Send a point P_inf of U to infinity, i.e. choose x with its only pole at P_inf.
- Following Weierstrass's normalisation, regard infinity as one point. The ideals are then those of the affine ring O(X - P_inf), so the relevant group is Pic(X - P_inf) = Pic^0(X), i.e. the Jacobian.
- Form Weierstrass's prime functions vanishing at the points representing the given class. These are analytic on X - P_inf, with an essential singularity at P_inf, and contain exponentials of everywhere-convergent power series.
- (Continued on the next page.) Truncate those everywhere-convergent power series. This gives an algebraic function g on X.
- g keeps (approximately) the prescribed zeros. Its extra zeros come from the truncated exponentials; zeros of partial sums of exp(w) have |w| of order N, so they lie near P_inf, i.e. in U.
- Hence the prescribed divisor is equivalent, in the affine ring, to the inverse of a product of points in U. Applying this to the inverse class gives the claim.
- Modern proof: the image of Sym^g(U) in J contains an open set V; finitely many translates/sums kV cover the compact connected group J.
errors: (1) This is only a programme, and as stated it does not work. For irrational algebraic a = sqrt2, binomial(a,k) = a(a-1)...(a-k+1)/k! has denominator k!. The denominators of the approximants therefore grow like n!^c, which swamps the geometric decay of the error at z = -1. This is why Thue-Siegel Pade methods work for rational exponents (where the denominator is about q^k * k-independent) but not for 2^{sqrt2}. Irrationality and transcendence of 2^{sqrt2} needed Gelfond's new method (Kuzmin 1930; Gelfond-Schneider 1934).

(2) As stated ('alle' relatively abelian fields) the claim is false. Division points of the ordinary Jacobian give only the unramified abelian extensions. Ramified ones, e.g. Kummer extensions of C(x), where genus 0 means there are no abelian functions at all, need generalized Jacobians (Rosenlicht 1954; Serre, Groupes algebriques et corps de classes). Tacitly 'unverzweigt' must be meant.

(3) If 'Klasse' meant a divisor class on the compact surface (degree fixed), the claim would fail: Sym^n(U) has small image in Pic^n. It is correct only because of the device in the proof: putting a point of U at infinity, so that the classes are ideal classes of the affine ring O(X - P_inf). Hilbert's proof sketch also leaves implicit why the truncated function's zeros approximate the prescribed ones exactly up to equivalence. The claim actually needs zeros exactly at the prescribed points; this holds if one truncates only the exponential factor of each prime function, keeping the algebraic factor that carries the zero.
Minor: 'ein Product ergeben, dass in ...' should grammatically be 'das'.

results.what: Simultaneous rational (Hermite-Pade type II) approximation of (1-z)^a and (1-z)^{-a} with common denominator proposed as a route to irrationality of 2^{sqrt2}
results.modern_name: Hermite-Pade approximation / Thue-Siegel method applied to Hilbert's 7th problem
results.usually_credited_to: Hermite (1873), Pade (1892) for the approximants; Thue (1909) and Siegel (1921, 1929) for the arithmetic use with binomial functions; irrationality and transcendence of 2^{sqrt2} by Kuzmin (1930) and Gelfond-Schneider (1934)

results.what: Division values of abelian functions generate all (unramified) abelian extensions of an algebraic function field
results.modern_name: Geometric (unramified) class field theory via the Jacobian; function-field Kronecker Jugendtraum
results.usually_credited_to: Classical over C (Riemann/Weber-era covering theory); algebraic form by Lang (1956), Rosenlicht and Serre (1950s) for the ramified case

results.what: Every ideal class of the affine ring of a Riemann surface contains a product of prime ideals at points of any prescribed small region; proved via Weierstrass prime functions and truncation of everywhere-convergent series
results.modern_name: Divisor classes represented by divisors supported in an open set (Jacobi inversion / openness of the Abel-Jacobi map, Runge-type approximation)
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore, following Abel-Jacobi-Riemann; Weierstrass prime functions (Weierstrass, 1870s-80s lectures)

deep.surprise_reason: Hilbert said publicly in 1900 that the irrationality of 2^{sqrt2} seemed very hard. A private note proposing a concrete Hermite-Pade simultaneous-approximation attack is a notable unpublished detail; it anticipates the Thue-Siegel style of approach. But it is only a suggestion and does not work as stated. The function-field class field note fits his known 12th-problem outlook. The third item is routine.

checkable.asserts: (1-(a+1)z/2)/(1-(1-a)z/2) is the [1/1] Pade approximant of (1-z)^a (error O(z^3))
the [1/1] Pade approximant of (1-z)^(-a) is the reciprocal of that of (1-z)^a, i.e. conjugate under a -> -a
the specialisation z=-1, a=sqrt2 gives 2^{sqrt2} (and 2^{-sqrt2} for the companion function)
the denominators of binomial(sqrt2,k) grow like k! (the obstruction to the naive Pade argument)
